ex1:
**Interpretation:** The researchers are right. The Neighbors mailer cost **$6,000** for 20,000 households and produced about **3,106** additional votes (38,201 voters × 8.13 points), so each vote cost **$1.93**. The staffer divided a cost *per household* ($0.30) by an effect *per voter* (8.1 points). Each household holds about **1.91** registered voters, so one 30-cent mailer reaches almost two voters, and the staffer's **$3.70** (3.69 before rounding) is too high by that factor. The cost and the effect must describe the same people. By effect the mailers rank Neighbors (+8.1), Self (+4.9), Hawthorne (+2.6), Civic Duty (+1.8); by cost per vote they rank the same way: **$1.93**, **$3.24**, **$6.10**, **$8.77**. The rankings agree only because every mailer had the same price and almost the same number of voters per household, so the cost per vote depends on the effect alone. They would differ when tactics have different prices: a tactic with a bigger effect per person but a much higher cost per person can still produce more expensive votes.

*Grading notes:* full credit needs (1) the four costs per vote, with $1.93 matching the paper, (2) the household-versus-voter mismatch, with about 1.91 voters per household, (3) the two rankings and why they agree (same price), and (4) a situation where they would differ. Common error: dividing by 8.1 instead of 0.081, which makes a vote 100 times too cheap. Strong answers add that the 30 cents covers only printing and postage, and that the effect was measured in a primary among people who had voted in 2004, so it may not carry over to another election.
ex2:
**Interpretation:** No. Raleigh's own 95% interval runs from about **−2.6 to +2.8** points: it cannot rule out zero, but it cannot rule out an effect larger than the other cities' either. A null result from a noisy study is not evidence of no effect. Raleigh's estimate is imprecise (precision **0.51**, against **2.37** for the five cities), so it gets only about **18%** of the weight. The updated belief is **+2.06** points (SE **0.59**), with an interval from **+0.9 to +3.2**. Priced in Raleigh at $0.56 per person on the list, a vote costs **$557.50** on Raleigh's estimate alone, **$22.48** on the five-city estimate and **$27.09** on the updated belief. I would not stop canvassing on the strength of this one result, and I would plan on roughly $27 a vote. The weakness is the assumption that every city has the same true effect. Raleigh had the highest contact rate in the study (44.6%) and still the smallest effect, which hints that something there (the voters, the election, the canvassers' message) may differ. If so, Raleigh's own result deserves more weight than its precision gives it, and before spending a lot I would run a larger test in Raleigh.

*Grading notes:* full credit needs (1) Raleigh's interval and the point that it includes both zero and large effects, (2) the weights, updated estimate and interval, (3) the three costs per vote, and (4) the same-effect assumption with a reason it might fail in Raleigh and what that means for the advice. Common errors: averaging 2.48 and 0.1 equally (+1.29), or using SE instead of SE² in the precision. Strong answers name the Week 5 point: a null result from an underpowered study is not evidence of no effect. The updated +2.06 (SE 0.59) is close to the study's All sites row (+2.1, SE 0.6) because it combines the same six cities; strong answers may notice this.
ex3:
**Interpretation:** The vendor's arithmetic is right: three rounds cost **$18,002** and produce about **1,718** votes, an average of **$10.48** a vote. But the average is the wrong number for this decision. Round by round, votes cost **$6.11**, **$12.22** and **$24.45**. The first two rounds are cheaper than canvassing at $17.60; the third is not. I would send two rounds and move the third round's $6,000 to canvassing, which buys about **341** votes instead of the third round's **245**. Counting net votes changes the answer. If new mail voters break 55–45, each additional voter adds only 0.10 to the margin, so a net vote costs **$61.12**, **$122.23** and **$244.46** in rounds 1–3. Canvassing in neighborhoods that break 70–30 costs **$44.00** per net vote, cheaper than even the first round of mail. On these numbers I would put the money into targeted canvassing. But the reversal comes from the assumed targeting, not from the tactics: mailed to the same 70–30 neighborhoods, round 1 would cost **$15.28** per net vote and beat canvassing. The real lesson is to target, whatever the tactic. Two cautions: rounds 2 and 3 rest on an assumed effect, and the $17.60 comes from 2001 local elections at 2001 wages while the mail effect comes from a 2006 primary among people who had voted in 2004, so a result from one setting may not carry over to the other.

*Grading notes:* full credit needs (1) the cost per vote of each round and the average, (2) the difference between the average and the last vote, (3) a stopping point (two rounds) with the money moved to canvassing, and (4) the net-vote costs and why they reverse the choice. Common errors: comparing the average ($10.48) with $17.60 and buying all three rounds; dividing by 0.55 instead of 0.55 − 0.45. Strong answers see that the net-vote reversal comes from the assumed splits (mail to 70–30 neighborhoods: $6.11 ÷ 0.40 = $15.28 per net vote) and note the different settings of the two studies.
